What the differences mean

  • K1 Max + Raptor: $549.00 + $879.00 = $1,428.00 separately; $1,428.00 − $1,258.20 = $169.80, or 11.9%. The store's label says $1,039.80, about 6 times the real figure.
  • K2 Pro Combo + Raptor Pro: $749.00 + $1,499.00 = $2,248.00; $2,248.00 − $2,009.00 = $239.00, or 10.6%. The label says $539.00.
  • K2 Plus + Raptor Pro: with the CFS, $1,099.00 + $1,499.00 = $2,598.00, a saving of $389.00 (15.0%). Without it, $899.00 + $1,499.00 = $2,398.00, a saving of $189.00 (7.9%). The label says $589.00.
  • Seal Lite + QIDI Q2: $215 + $449 = $664, which is $1,258.20 − $664 = $594.20 less than the cheapest Creality combo.
  • Moose Lite + QIDI Q2: $239 + $449 = $688.

Why a combo doesn't buy you a better scan-to-print workflow

In these combos the scanner and the printer never connect to each other. Creality's own CR-Scan Otter guide describes the steps: plug the scanner into a computer's USB 3.0 port and scan in CrealityScan. Then export the model as STL and open it in the Creality Print slicer, which sends it to the printer. For that scanner the computer needs Windows 10/11 64-bit (at least an 8th-gen Intel i5 with 8 GB RAM, 16 GB recommended) or macOS 10.15.7 or later. Any printer that accepts an STL file fits these steps, so the box adds nothing technically. What it adds is a discount, and on today's prices that discount is $169.80–$389.00. The 'Save' labels look bigger because they're measured against compare-at prices. For example, the K1 Max + Raptor's $2,298 compare-at is $870 above the $1,428 the two parts cost on their own today.

Not recommended

Creality Otter Lite + 3D Printer (All-In-One Combo), $1,606. Its product page doesn't name the printer and its 'Combo Details' section is empty. With the Otter Lite at $759 on its own, $847 of the price goes to a printer you can't identify before you pay. The same Otter Lite plus a QIDI Q2, a named enclosed 270 × 270 × 256 mm printer, costs $759 + $449 = $1,208, which is $398 less.
